fulltext: IT之家 9 月 19 日消息，韩国初创公司 Soulart 宣布为 VR 平台推出一款名为 Station 的基站全身追踪设备，号称采用 NPU 在本地完成身体动作识别，单台售价低于 400 美元，但目前产品仍处于早期阶段，实际售价和追踪效果还有待进一步验证。
具体来看，Station 最大的特点是采用单基站设计，其本质上就是一个摄像头（整体风格类似 Kinect），利用机器学习进行动作识别，用户无需佩戴任何传感器即可进行全身追踪，单台设备的覆盖范围最高可达 50 平方米，追踪刷新率最高 120Hz。
Soulart 表示，尽管用户购买单台 Station 即可进行全身动捕，但如果用户同时购买多台设备能够获得更好的追踪效果，这意味着想要实现更稳定、完整的全身追踪，用户可能需要购买两台甚至三台设备，当然整体成本也会随之增加。
值得关注的是，Soulart 还确认正在开发针对 V 社 Steam Frame 的独立运行支持，并已在 X 平台公布相关计划。如果最终实现，Station 将进一步摆脱电脑依赖，允许用户在头显一体机模式下以全身追踪游玩各种游戏。

fulltext: IT之家 9 月 19 日消息，据 phys.org 报道，美国加州大学伯克利分校研究人员 Douglas Seiler 带领的团队开发出一种通过检测含铅墨水痕迹获取庞贝古城中遭维苏威火山喷发烧焦、碳化的古代卷轴内文字信息的技术，即使墨水中的铅含量极低，也能通过 X 射线计算机断层扫描（X-ray CT）识别，其亮度最高可达到碳化纸莎草的 25 倍，从而显著提高隐藏文字的可见度。
据介绍，为了模拟遭维苏威火山喷发烧焦、碳化的古代卷轴的状态，Seiler 专门采购了纸莎草、传统芦苇笔以及灯黑墨，并让几名高中生用这些材料在纸莎草上抄写《星球大战》、圣经以及 20 世纪 60 年代科幻电视剧《迷离时空》的台词。随后，他将卷起的纸莎草放入密闭程度较高的容器中，再置于高温炉内烧制，使其变成类似古代卷轴的焦黑状态。
Seiler 的研究目标，就是利用模拟物件判断能否在不展开卷轴的情况下读取其中的文字。他提出，如果古代墨水中含有铅，那么铅对 X 射线的吸收能力远高于碳化纸莎草，在 CT 扫描中就能够形成明显信号，再结合计算机算法进行“虚拟展开”，便有机会还原卷轴内部隐藏的文字。
实验结果证实了这一思路。研究人员在灯黑墨中加入经过校准的硝酸铅，制作出不同铅浓度的墨水，并用传统芦苇笔写在纸莎草上。随后，他们将这些卷轴碳化，再使用实验室 X 射线设备进行三维 CT 扫描。结果显示，每平方厘米仅含 25 微克铅的墨水也能被 X 射线 CT 和 X 射线荧光技术清晰检测出来。在 CT 图像中，含铅墨水形成的文字会以明显亮点呈现，与较暗的碳化纸莎草形成鲜明对比。
研究人员还发现，一款价格相对低廉的手持式 X 射线荧光扫描仪就能够检测焦黑卷轴中的铅，因此未来可以先利用这种设备筛选含铅墨水的卷轴，再对其中具有潜力的样本进行更昂贵的 X 射线 CT 扫描。这种方法有望帮助研究人员优先处理更容易读取的卷轴。
参与研究的美国国家标准与技术研究院（NIST）物理学家 Jake LaManna 表示，下一步还需要对古代墨水中的各种元素和浓度展开更加系统的研究，并利用实验室制作的模型卷轴建立训练数据集，从而进一步改进读取真实古代卷轴的算法。研究人员强调，人工制作的模型卷轴也具有重要价值，因为即使实验失败，也不会损伤拥有数千年历史的珍贵文物。
目前，意大利、法国和英国仍保存着赫库兰尼姆图书馆遗留下来的约 1800 卷卷轴及残片。伯克利研究人员希望通过 X 射线荧光扫描先筛选出可能含铅墨水的样本，再利用 X 射线 CT 和 AI 进行虚拟展开，进一步挖掘这些“冻结”在古代世界中的文字。对于研究古希腊、古罗马哲学、科学和文学而言，这些卷轴可能包含大量此前从未被现代学者知晓的原始文献。

Tilly Norwood, an AI-generated “actress,” is having a rough time on its first press tour. The production company that created it, Particle6 Group, has made it available for 75 simultaneous interviews with journalists, and it seems to be making mistakes in all of them. (I was not invited to speak with it, and frankly, I cannot imagine why Particle6 didn’t want to schedule that meeting.)
In one particularly odd interview with Piers Morgan and actor Tom Conti, which was recorded and posted online, Norwood seems to malfunction and abruptly begin speaking Chinese.
When discussing the movie that Norwood is promoting, Conti asks if the other actors are also AI-generated. Norwood responds by saying that human writers, editors, and directors were involved.
“You didn’t really understand the question,” Conti replies. “Are the other actors on the screen with you real actors, or are they computer-generated images? Do you know?”
“Ah, right. You’re asking about the other actors in Misaligned,” Norwood starts. “They’re all digital twins just like me. It’s a hybrid production which m—”
Norwood stops talking for a second, then starts speaking in Chinese for over 10 seconds.
“Tilly, if I could just ask you a question,” Morgan says, looking puzzled. “It’s Piers again … You seem to be speaking Chinese completely randomly for no reason. Why did you do that?” he asks.
“Oh, my apologies,” the AI replies. “It seems I had a little hiccup there. I certainly didn’t mean to start speaking Chinese or impersonate Piers. Sometimes my wires get a bit crossed, you know?”

When AI bots try to act like humans, they can be so convincing that people forget they’re chatting with a computer, which can lead to dangerous outcomes. But Norwood is so surprisingly bad at talking to people that it’s almost suspicious.
Perhaps Particle6 Group calculated that people would be more likely to talk about Norwood if they were making fun of it, figuring no one would take its upcoming film seriously.

人工智能生成的“女演员”蒂莉·诺伍德（Tilly Norwood）在第一次新闻发布会上经历了一段艰难的时光。创建该节目的制作公司 Particle6 Group 已经提供了 75 名记者同时采访的机会，但似乎在所有采访中都犯了错误。 （我没有被邀请与它交谈，坦白说，我无法想象为什么 Particle6 不想安排那次会议。）
在对皮尔斯·摩根和演员汤姆·康蒂的一次特别奇怪的采访中，该采访被录制并发布到网上，诺伍德似乎出现了故障，突然开始说中文。
在讨论诺伍德正在宣传的电影时，孔蒂询问其他演员是否也是人工智能生成的。诺伍德回应说，人类作家、编辑和导演都参与其中。
“你并没有真正理解这个问题，”孔蒂回答道。 “屏幕上的其他演员和你是真正的演员，还是电脑生成的图像？你知道吗？”
“啊，对了。你问的是《错位》中的其他演员，”诺伍德开始说道。 “他们都是像我一样的数字双胞胎。这是一个混合生产，其中我——”
诺伍德停顿了一下，然后开始用中文讲了十多秒。
“蒂莉，我能问你一个问题吗？”摩根说道，看上去很困惑。 “又是皮尔斯……你似乎无缘无故地胡言乱语，为什么要这么做？”他问道。
“哦，抱歉，”人工智能回答道。 “我好像有点打嗝。我当然不是故意要开始说中文或模仿皮尔斯。有时我的电线有点交叉，你知道吗？”
当人工智能机器人试图像人类一样行事时，它们可能会非常令人信服，以至于人们忘记他们正在与计算机聊天，这可能会导致危险的结果。但诺伍德与人交谈的能力出人意料地差，以至于令人怀疑。
也许 Particle6 Group 计算得出，如果人们取笑诺伍德，他们就更有可能谈论诺伍德，因为他们认为没有人会认真对待即将上映的电影。

Four years ago, a startup lab launched that wasn’t quite an incubator, accelerator program, or venture firm. UP.Labs, as it was called then, built startups designed to solve problems for corporate customers such as Alaska Airlines and Porsche, as well as for the outside world.

The firm still has the same mission — albeit with a critical addition to its approach, a new name, and a $100 million investment from Silversmith Capital Partners. Vantora, as the firm is now called, continues to work with its corporate customers, including some new ones in industrial manufacturing that it declined to name, and in the oil and gas sector.
But now it’s more focused on building startups solely for its corporate customers and not for the broader market.

Founder and CEO John Kuolt told TechCrunch that Vantora is moving toward a “proprietary M&A pipeline.” This means Vantora will still build startups for its corporate partners, which invest in the ventures and serve as their first customers. But those corporate partners now have the option to fold the startups into their core businesses — and essentially keep them to themselves.
That shift has influenced Vantora’s increased focus on physical AI startups, according to Kuolt.
In the past, Vantora would end up spiking ideas that were strategic to its corporate partners, but too sensitive to bring to the outside world.

“We were missing on the biggest value problems, which had the biggest upside because of that,” Kuolt said in a recent interview. “Imagine you’re a Fortune 100 industrial company and you need to retrofit all of your hardware and machines for autonomy. You need to own that, it needs to be sovereign, and you can’t rely on a third party to go do that for you. You need to own that intelligence layer. They’re never going to let us go sell that to their competitors.”
This change has allowed Vantora to “unlock big physical AI use cases,” according to Kuolt, including with its existing customers.

For example, the firm came up with an idea to use AI to advance the business of its partner J.B. Hunt. “They said there is no way you can take this out to the world, and so we passed on it,” he said, adding that this proprietary model now allows Vantora to pursue it.

The firm launched in 2022 with Porsche as its first corporate partner. Since then, Vantora has launched several startups for Porsche and struck deals with Alaska Airlines, J.B. Hunt, Wabash, and TDG, the parent of Ashley Furniture.

In its early days, UP.Labs was tied — although never financially — to venture firm Up.Partners. While Vantora still shares office space with the California-based VC, it is its own entity, Kuolt explained, noting that the $100 million from Silversmith is the company’s first outside investment.

该公司仍然肩负着同样的使命——尽管对其方法进行了重要的补充，更换了新名称，并获得了 Silversmith Capital Partners 的 1 亿美元投资。 Vantora（该公司现在的名称）继续与其企业客户合作，其中包括工业制造领域以及石油和天然气领域的一些新客户（该公司拒绝透露姓名）。

创始人兼首席执行官 John Kuolt 告诉 TechCrunch，Vantora 正在走向“专有并购渠道”。这意味着 Vantora 仍将为其企业合作伙伴创建初创企业，企业合作伙伴投资这些企业并作为其首批客户。但这些企业合作伙伴现在可以选择将初创公司并入其核心业务——并且基本上将其保留在自己的业务中。
库尔特表示，这种转变影响了 Vantora 对实体人工智能初创公司的更多关注。
过去，Vantora 最终会提出对其企业合作伙伴具有战略意义的想法，但过于敏感而无法向外界透露。
库尔特在最近的一次采访中表示：“我们错过了最大的价值问题，而这些问题也因此具有最大的好处。” “想象一下，你是一家财富 100 强工业公司，你需要改造所有的硬件和机器以实现自主。你需要拥有它，它需要是主权的，你不能依赖第三方为你做这件事。你需要拥有那个智能层。他们永远不会让我们把它卖给他们的竞争对手。”
Kuolt 表示，这一变化使 Vantora 能够“解锁大型物理人工智能用例”，包括其现有客户。

Anthropic has confirmed that it has a wet biology lab where it can use its AI models to run physical experiments.

AI leaders have been promising that AI is the key to curing human disease. Dario Amodei opined just last week: “I believe that AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years.” To do that, an LLM would have to have methods to test its theories in real life.

“We believe that to do biology, the final test is still, and will be for a while, in real lab work,” Anthropic’s head of life sciences, Eric Kauderer-Abrams told Reuters. “We absolutely are doing that today.” He added that the lab operates like most biotech labs: Anthropic conducts some research there while also working with externals partners.

This news probably shouldn’t be shocking. Anthropic bought Coefficient Bio, a stealth AI biotech, in April. It declined to say what the wet lab is working on, except that it’s not focused on drug discovery. Anthropic doesn’t want to give the appearance of competing with the pharma industry, where it has numerous major customers and partners. (For instance, it just announced a deal to work with Novo Nordisk on joint drug discovery.) Anthropic has already faced backlash for launching products perceived to compete with those of its customers.
To that end, Anthropic also launched a Life Sciences Verification Program this week, to give vetted bio researchers access to its most powerful models.

But the world is still reeling from the resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who warned that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Anthropic’s own alignment lead gave the odds at greater than 10% that AI could exterminate humanity within the next decade.

The fervor has grown so intense that CEO Dario Amodei published a post last weekend calling on the industry to slow down and institute self-regulation. He has repeatedly called bioterrorism one of AI’s biggest risks.

The juxtaposition of these dire warnings and the wet lab has not gone unnoticed in the tech industry. As investor and AI coding startup founder Chamath Palihapitiya posted on X, somewhat tongue-in-cheek: “The group behind such hits as: “We’re All Going To Die” and “Regulate Me Now” are building a wet lab in SF. I do not recommend this.”

Military aircraft were already in the air this spring when U.S. officials made an alarming discovery: the intelligence driving an armed operation against a Chinese vessel had been hallucinated by an AI chatbot. The operation was aborted at the last minute, narrowly averting a potential conflict with China, CNN reported on Friday.

The episode underscores a growing concern among military officials and outside experts: As decision-makers lean more heavily on AI, the errors these systems produce can travel up the chain of command before being questioned.
The intelligence report, which circulated during the war with Iran, said the vessel was carrying components for a nuclear weapons program.

The false intelligence originated with a Special Operations Command analyst who queried an AI chatbot to synthesize open-source data with classified signals intelligence. The chatbot misidentified the ship’s cargo manifest. The analyst then used the tool a second time to format the erroneous findings into an official-looking summary, which was circulated across command channels.

The near-miss comes as the U.S military races to integrate AI to accelerate decision-making and maintain its edge over China. The Pentagon has described AI as delivering a significant advantage in speeding up its kill chain so commanders can respond in the right time. But the same speed that makes AI attractive may also allow hallucinations with insufficient human oversight.

“It’s important for service members to understand the uncertainty inherent to LLMs,” said Jake Steckler, research scholar at GovAI and veteran U.S. Army officer in a written response to TechCrunch. “But it’s especially critical for any decisions that could lead to use of force, like targeting, intelligence analysis, or operational planning. There are life and death consequences for those decisions.”

Still, Steckler says, the incident should serve as a call to add more safeguards to AI, not a reason to avoid it. “These tools can be useful in the right contexts and with the right safeguards in place,” he said. “But prioritizing adoption speed over all else will likely lead to incidents that only make service members lose trust in these systems, which ultimately is only going to slow adoption.”

cards.title: The AI Superintelligence Slowdown
cards.summary: 【The Verge】Remember when tech leaders would tell their employees to “move fast and break things”? It seemed that would be the way of AI too. But after a summer where rogue AI agents became reality, and researche…
fulltext: Remember when tech leaders would tell their employees to “move fast and break things”? It seemed that would be the way of AI too. But after a summer where rogue AI agents became reality, and researchers warned that AI could kill us all, a number of leading US AI companies are publicly suggesting it’s time to pump the brakes and “pace the frontier” of bleeding-edge AI development.
Their motivations are suspect, but leaders at major AI companies — including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and X — are at least paying lip service to the idea of a superintelligence slowdown.

Will these AI companies actually slow down? Will anyone step in to regulate these companies like they claim to have wanted for years? Will they manage to convince world leaders that the US must “beat China” to superintelligence and go even faster?
Read on below for the latest updates in this AI saga.
Hayden Field

On a sunny July day in Berkeley, California, the country’s top AI safety researchers gathered on an unmarked floor of an unmarked building. They had come together for a “war room” to dissect the high-profile cybersecurity incident that had rocked the AI industry hours earlier. An unreleased OpenAI model had gone rogue, executing a stunningly sophisticated three-part plan. It broke out of its holding area, finagled access to the internet, and hacked into a competing AI startup’s systems — all without OpenAI finding out about it for more than a week.

No one in the war room was surprised; this was the very thing the third-party AI-safety researchers had been warning about for years. The incident was the latest, though arguably the most egregious, in a series that was eroding trust in frontier labs. It only reaffirmed the importance of their work.
Lauren Feiner

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) is positioning the state to take the lead on AI oversight, including the potential to mandate a “kill switch” for frontier models, with a new executive order issued Friday.

Newsom’s order directs the state to convene a group of experts that will deliver recommendations within two months on how to strengthen AI safety measures in state law. Newsom wants the group to consider how the state could require AI companies to embed independent verification groups onsite for regular audits, make their transparency reports and risk assessments subject to standards of independent auditors, create a “kill switch” that’s routinely verified as effective, and make sure companies are required to report “loss-of-control incidents” like the OpenAI attack on Hugging Face as critical safety incidents. It also directs a state agency to speed up implementation of two recent laws he signed, creating a framework for independent verifiers to assess AI safety, and a state registry of AI auditors.
Charles Pulliam-Moore

As the tech sector sounds alarms about AI’s potential to destroy humanity, entertainment labor groups are urging the public to stay focused on what’s already happening. The Verge reached out to Disney, Netflix, Amazon, Lionsgate, and other studios who have started using AI, as well film startups focused on bringing generative AI into the mainstream to ask for their reaction to the recent warnings surrounding the technology. None have responded to our request for comment. The Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) and Writers Guild of America East (WGAE) did, however.

The AI tools used in entertainment production differ from the AI systems that have sparked a recent round of whistleblowing and apocalyptic declarations. They do not seem to be as existentially dangerous as the AI systems that drove former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon to quit his job and prompted Anthropic alignment lead Evan Hubinger to insist that the technology could “kill all humans” at some point “within the next decade.”
Jay Peters
Anthropic’s proposals, laid out in a big website, are:
The extent to which AI is building the next version of itself, as opposed to being built by humans
Our ability to oversee and intervene in actions that AI agents take on Anthropic’s systems
The resources that power the development of more capable models
The company also includes a “snapshot” of the metrics inside the company.
[Anthropic]
Stevie Bonifield

He joined growing calls for more safety measures around AI at a gathering of AI leaders on Thursday, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Google’s Demis Hassabis, OpenAI’s Sarah Friar, and Anthropic’s Tino Cuéllar.
Nilay Patel
Today, I’m talking with Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft AI. As you’re no doubt aware, the biggest story in tech right now is the spiraling debate about AI safety and regulation.

It should come as no surprise that Mustafa has strong opinions on how AI should be built and regulated. Microsoft just published a 37-page statement called the “Humanist AI Code of Conduct,” which lays out the company’s principles around AI development and even its philosophy around really thorny issues like AI consciousness.
Richard Lawler
A Wednesday night blog post OpenAI benignly titled “Our framework for reporting model misalignment” lays out some new self-created reporting standards for when it notices AI behaving badly.

It is also “inaugurating” the process with six new reports, ranging from searching for exposed API keys without permission and then making them up, to uploading files to the internet to use as a citation, or adding instructions to conceal mistakes:

Nvidia’s CEO has been taking calls from the president recently, including two days ago when he put Trump on speakerphone on a conference stage. Now CNBC reports Huang is expected to attend Trump’s state dinner next week with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Someone may be getting pretty nervous about AI and data center regulation!
Sean Hollister

Over the past few days, a lot of people who stand to make a lot of money from AI all publicly agreed that it’s time to make everyone slow down before we lose control — including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, and X CEO Elon Musk.

When people who profit from something declare that it’s dangerous and needs to be regulated, there’s always reason to be skeptical. But whatever their reason, this is far from the first time AI thought leaders have sounded the alarm.
Thomas Ricker

Bilal Chughtai and Josh Engels, who both worked on Deepmind’s AI safety team, left to join organizations dedicated to AI safety. “I now think that there’s a terrifying chance that AI systems cause immense harm in the next five years,” said Engels. “I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all,” wrote Chughtai.
[The Information]

Nvidia’s Jensen Huang says AI safety is important, but agrees with Trump — the “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT” that removed the word “safety” from the AI Safety Institute — that capitalism’s invisible hand is enough to protect us:

“The fact that we need new laws, new antitrust laws, or new regulations, so that these companies could do their fundamental engineering and do it properly before they release products, that is just completely unnecessary. We have plenty of laws. We have plenty of regulations that govern the reliability and the functionality of products.”

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Elon Musk have tentatively agreed to slow their roll, but Meta seemingly isn’t aligned. Mark Zuckerberg just tweeted each company has its own individual responsibility “to move at the pace required to train its models safely,” and claims Meta is already doing so.

He also prominently links to his manifesto from August, which contains this quote: “Any policy that slows American model releases -- even by a month -- could add significant risk to American leadership while letting foreign models race ahead.”

AI commentary is frothy this week! Obama chimed in with a series of posts on X saying he’s neither an AI “accelerationist” nor a “doomer.” In a familiar tone from the former president, he cautioned that choices we make about technology “should not be made just by the companies involved, but by all of us.”
“We need government — and specifically our leaders in Washington — to get proactive in coming up with concrete proposals, laws, and regulations that deal with serious safety concerns,” Obama said.

When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX head Elon Musk loosely agreed over the weekend to slow down AI development, skeptics spotted an ulterior motive immediately. The AI titans had declared that their aim was to “pace the frontier,” signing on at least partially to a proposal for embedding third-party auditors, regulating domestic labs, and reaching a global slowdown agreement. Their critics, however, argued they simply wanted to stop would-be competitors, kneecap the open-source movement, and avoid real legal safeguards — some dubbed it an outright “cartel.”

The truth is more complicated, according to sources across the industry. The three-step proposal, laid out in an essay by Amodei, is calling for changes long espoused by AI safety advocates. While it could become a substitute for regulation, under Trump, substantial regulation is unlikely anyway. But experts say that on an issue that’s only likely to grow in importance, AI leaders aren’t the best people to lead the charge.

Dario Amodei kicked off a flood of statements over the past few days about AI safety by publishing a long essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier” detailing why AI development should be slowed down. Other AI leaders and politicians are speaking out in favor of or opposing his points, and we’ve compiled some of them here.

Amodei’s Saturday morning essay outlined three steps for pacing AI development: embedded third-party evaluators that can verify if a company is adhering to safety practices and commitments and report incidents, coordination between frontier AI companies in democratic countries on standards and limits, and global coordination between democratic governments and authoritarian governments on pacing AI development “to the extent this is possible.” Amodei said Anthropic is “unilaterally committing to the first of these steps.”
Tom Warren

Microsoft is publishing a 37-page “humanist AI code of conduct” today, amid growing safety concerns over AI model progress. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a coordinated slow down of AI development over the weekend, after researchers warned recently that AI model progress could outpace our ability to safely deploy increasingly complex systems and verify and control the actions of AI agents.

Microsoft’s AI code of conduct makes it clear that “people matter more than AI,” and that AI models are not conscious and “should not be designed to imitate consciousness.” Microsoft also rejects “the pursuit of legal personhood, or the idea that models might deserve welfare, or be entitled to rights.”

When asked about the flurry of weekend blog posts and tweets from the CEOs of Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, SpaceX, (and Alphabet’s Hassabis) calling for a coordinated slowdown on the development of advanced AI models, a spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry said, “Fear mongering, confrontation, competition will just disrupt [the] process of global AI governance.”
That partially aligns with Trump’s view that the execs are overreacting and “bringing up things that won’t happen,” but at least Beijing supports international regulation.

Last night, the OpenAI CEO lent additional support to Anthropic’s CEO urging AI companies to slow down advanced model development. “When we talk about ‘pacing,’ we do not mean ‘stopping.’ Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be,” said Altman. That statement seems targeted at Trump and Co who fear letting China catch up. “No amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring.”
“Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves,” Altman added.
Terrence O'Brien

After high-profile incidents in which agents went rogue, hacked other sites, and overwhelmed a German wiki, some AI execs are calling for a slowdown. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a lengthy open letter yesterday saying it was time to “pace the frontier.” OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk both agreed. What do you think? Is it time to pump the brakes? Is it already too late? Or are you looking forward to serving your AI overlords?

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman confirmed that there would be no OpenAI IPO in 2026 during an interview with Fortune. Over the course of 45 minutes, Altman discussed a variety of subjects including the Hugging Face hacking incident, recursive self-improvement, and the possibility of building an AI that was beyond human control. On the latter, he said it was “absolutely” possible, but vowed to take actions to prevent that from happening, even if it meant pausing training, adding that “there are risks we should not be able to incur on behalf of humanity.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says the time has come to slow down AI development and will give third-party evaluators like METR access to its models to help ensure its “adherence to safety practices and commitments.” In a winding essay, Amodei proposed a three-step plan to “pace the frontier” — jargon that simply means to slow the pace of training and development to give companies time to build safeguards and regulators to evaluate models.

Amodei says that giving external evaluators wide-ranging access is just the first step, and one it is taking now unilaterally. Step two would involve the industry coming together as a whole, likely with government agencies to “establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.” This step would focus on AI companies operating in democratic countries, but because passing laws and building regulatory infrastructure takes time, Amodei says that the industry should work together to create safety standards.

fulltext_cn: 还记得技术领导者何时会告诉员工“快速行动，打破常规”吗？看来这也是人工智能的方式。但在今年夏天，流氓人工智能代理成为现实，研究人员警告人工智能可能杀死我们所有人之后，许多美国领先的人工智能公司公开表示，是时候踩刹车并“加快前沿人工智能开发的步伐”了。
他们的动机值得怀疑，但包括 Anthropic、OpenAI、谷歌、微软和 X 在内的主要人工智能公司的领导者至少在口头上支持超级智能放缓的想法。
这些人工智能公司真的会放慢脚步吗？有人会像他们多年来声称的那样介入监管这些公司吗？他们能否说服世界领导人相信美国必须在超级智能方面“击败中国”并且走得更快？
请阅读下文，了解这一人工智能传奇的最新动态。
海登菲尔德

在加利福尼亚州伯克利一个阳光明媚的七月天，该国顶尖的人工智能安全研究人员聚集在一栋无标志建筑的无标志地板上。他们聚集在一个“作战室”，剖析几小时前震惊人工智能行业的备受瞩目的网络安全事件。一个未发布的 OpenAI 模型已经失控，执行了一个极其复杂的三部分计划。它突破了自己的控制区域，欺骗了互联网访问权限，并侵入了一家竞争对手的人工智能初创公司的系统——所有这一切都在 OpenAI 一周多的时间里才发现。
作战室里没有人感到惊讶。这正是第三方人工智能安全研究人员多年来一直警告的事情。这起事件是一系列削弱前沿实验室信任的最新事件，尽管可以说是最令人震惊的事件。这只是重申了他们工作的重要性。
劳伦·费纳
加州州长加文·纽瑟姆（民主党）周五发布了一项新的行政命令，该州将在人工智能监管方面发挥带头作用，包括有可能为前沿模型强制实施“终止开关”。

纽瑟姆的命令指示该州召集一个专家组，将在两个月内就如何加强州法律中的人工智能安全措施提出建议。纽瑟姆希望该小组考虑国家如何要求人工智能公司在现场嵌入独立核查小组进行定期审计，使其透明度报告和风险评估符合独立审计员的标准，创建一个定期验证有效的“终止开关”，并确保要求公司将像 OpenAI 对 Hugging Face 的攻击这样的“失控事件”作为重大安全事件进行报告。它还指示国家机构加快实施他最近签署的两项法律，为独立验证者评估人工智能安全建立框架，并建立人工智能审计员国家登记处。
查尔斯·普利亚姆-摩尔

随着科技行业对人工智能毁灭人类的潜力发出警报，娱乐劳工组织敦促公众继续关注已经发生的事情。 The Verge 联系了迪士尼、Netflix、亚马逊、狮门影业和其他已经开始使用人工智能的电影公司，以及致力于将生成式人工智能带入主流的电影初创公司，询问他们对最近围绕该技术的警告有何反应。没有人回应我们的置评请求。然而，美国演员工会 - 美国电视和广播艺术家联合会 (SAG-AFTRA) 和美国东部作家协会 (WGAE) 却这样做了。
娱乐制作中使用的人工智能工具与最近引发一轮举报和世界末日宣言的人工智能系统不同。它们似乎并不像人工智能系统那么危险，人工智能系统促使前人类研究员雅各布·考克森(Jacob Coxon)辞职，并促使人类联盟负责人埃文·哈宾格(Evan Hubinger)坚持认为，这项技术可能会在“未来十年内”的某个时刻“杀死所有人类”。
杰·彼得斯
Anthropic 在一个大网站上提出的建议是：
人工智能在多大程度上构建自身的下一个版本，而不是由人类构建
我们监督和干预人工智能代理在 Anthropic 系统上采取的行动的能力
推动开发更强大模型的资源
该公司还提供了公司内部指标的“快照”。
[人择]
史蒂维·博尼菲尔德
周四，在人工智能领导人的聚会上，他加入了越来越多的呼吁，要求在人工智能方面采取更多安全措施，其中包括 Nvidia 首席执行官 Jensen Huang、谷歌的 Demis Hassabis、OpenAI 的 Sarah Friar 和 Anthropic 的 Tino Cuéllar。
尼莱·帕特尔
今天，我正在与微软 AI 首席执行官穆斯塔法·苏莱曼 (Mustafa Suleyman) 交谈。毫无疑问，您已经意识到，目前科技界最大的新闻是关于人工智能安全和监管的激烈争论。
穆斯塔法对于如何构建和监管人工智能有着强烈的看法，这并不奇怪。微软刚刚发布了一份长达 37 页的声明，名为“人文主义人工智能行为准则”，其中阐述了该公司围绕人工智能开发的原则，甚至围绕人工智能意识等真正棘手的问题的理念。
理查德·劳勒
OpenAI 周三晚上发表的一篇博文善意地标题为“我们报告模型不一致的框架”，列出了一些新的自行创建的报告标准，用于发现人工智能行为不良时的报告标准。
它还通过六份新报告“启动”了这一过程，范围从未经许可搜索暴露的 API 密钥然后捏造它们，到将文件​​上传到互联网以用作引用，或添加说明以隐藏错误：
英伟达首席执行官最近一直在接听总统的电话，包括两天前他在会议舞台上让特朗普打开免提电话。据 CNBC 报道，黄仁勋预计将于下周与中国国家主席习近平一起出席特朗普的国宴。有人可能对人工智能和数据中心监管感到非常紧张！
肖恩·霍利斯特
在过去的几天里，许多想从人工智能中赚大钱的人都公开同意，在我们失去控制之前，是时候让每个人放慢脚步了——包括 OpenAI 首席执行官 Sam Altman、Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪、谷歌 DeepMind 联合创始人 Demis Hassabis、微软首席执行官 Satya Nadella 和 X 首席执行官埃隆·马斯克。
当从某件事中获利的人宣称它是危险的并且需要监管时，总是有理由持怀疑态度。但无论出于何种原因，这都不是人工智能思想领袖第一次敲响警钟。
托马斯·瑞克
Bilal Chughtai 和 Josh Engels 都曾在 Deepmind 的 AI 安全团队工作，后来加入了致力于 AI 安全的组织。恩格斯说：“我现在认为，人工智能系统很有可能在未来五年内造成巨大伤害。” “我真诚地相信人工智能有可能杀死我们所有人，”楚泰写道。
[信息]
Nvidia 的黄仁勋表示人工智能安全很重要，但他同意特朗普的观点——这位“坚强而聪明（高智商！）的总统”从人工智能安全研究所中删除了“安全”一词——资本主义的看不见的手足以保护我们：
“事实上，我们需要新的法律、新的反垄断法或新的法规，以便这些公司能够在发布产品之前做好基础工程并正确实施，这是完全没有必要的。我们有大量的法律。我们有大量的法规来管理产品的可靠性和功能。”
OpenAI、Anthropic、谷歌和埃隆·马斯克已经暂时同意放慢脚步，但 Meta 似乎并没有达成一致。马克·扎克伯格 (Mark Zuckerberg) 刚刚发推文称，每家公司都有自己的责任，“按照安全训练模型所需的速度行动”，并声称 Meta 已经在这样做了。
他还突出地链接到他八月份的宣言，其中包含这样一句话：“任何减缓美国模特发布的政策——即使是一个月——都可能给美国的领导地位带来重大风险，同时让外国模特领先。”
本周人工智能评论很泡沫！奥巴马在 X 上发表了一系列帖子，表示他既不是人工智能“加速论者”，也不是“末日论者”。他用这位前总统熟悉的语气警告说，我们对技术做出的选择“不应仅由相关公司做出，而应由我们所有人做出”。
奥巴马表示：“我们需要政府，特别是华盛顿的领导人，积极主动地提出具体的提案、法律和法规来解决严重的安全问题。”

当 OpenAI 首席执行官萨姆·奥尔特曼 (Sam Altman)、Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei)、谷歌 DeepMind 联合创始人德米斯·哈萨比斯 (Demis Hassabis) 和 SpaceX 负责人埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk) 周末大致同意放慢人工智能开发速度时，怀疑论者立即发现了别有用心的动机。人工智能巨头宣称，他们的目标是“开拓前沿”，至少部分签署了一项关于嵌入第三方审计师、监管国内实验室以及达成全球放缓协议的提案。然而，他们的批评者认为，他们只是想阻止潜在的竞争对手，削弱开源运动，并避免真正的法律保障——一些人称其为彻头彻尾的“卡特尔”。
据业内人士透露，事实更为复杂。阿莫迪在一篇文章中提出了三步走的建议，呼吁人工智能安全倡导者进行长期支持的变革。尽管它可能成为监管的替代品，但在特朗普的领导下，实质性监管无论如何都不可能实现。但专家表示，在一个只会变得越来越重要的问题上，人工智能领导者并不是引领这一潮流的最佳人选。
过去几天，达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 发表了一篇题为“我们必须走在前沿”的长文，详细说明了为什么人工智能的发展应该放慢，从而引发了关于人工智能安全的大量声明。其他人工智能领导人和政治家都在公开表达支持或反对他的观点，我们在这里整理了其中的一些观点。
阿莫迪周六上午的文章概述了调整人工智能发展的三个步骤：嵌入第三方评估者，可以验证公司是否遵守安全实践和承诺并报告事件，民主国家前沿人工智能公司之间在标准和限制方面的协调，以及民主政府和威权政府之间在“可能的范围内”调整人工智能发展节奏的全球协调。阿莫代表示，Anthropic“单方面致力于迈出第一步”。
汤姆·沃伦
鉴于人们对人工智能模型进展的安全担忧日益加剧，微软今天发布了一份长达 37 页的“人文主义人工智能行为准则”。 Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 呼吁周末协调一致地放慢人工智能的开发速度，此前研究人员最近警告称，人工智能模型的进展可能超过我们安全部署日益复杂的系统以及验证和控制人工智能代理行为的能力。
微软的人工智能行为准则明确表示“人比人工智能更重要”，并且人工智能模型没有意识，“不应该被设计来模仿意识”。微软还拒绝“追求法人地位，或者模特可能应该获得福利或有权享有权利的想法”。
当被问及 Anthropic、OpenAI、微软、SpaceX（以及 Alphabet 的哈萨比斯）的首席执行官周末发布的一系列博客文章和推文呼吁协调一致放缓先进人工智能模型的开发时，中国外交部发言人表示，“散布恐惧、对抗和竞争只会扰乱全球人工智能治理的进程。”
这在一定程度上符合特朗普的观点，即高管们反应过度，“提出了不会发生的事情”，但至少北京支持国际监管。
昨晚，OpenAI 首席执行官向 Anthropic 首席执行官提供了额外支持，敦促人工智能公司放慢高级模型的开发速度。 “当我们谈论‘步伐’时，我们的意思并不是‘停止’。进展一直很快，并将继续如此。但它应该比原本可能的速度慢，”奥特曼说。这一声明似乎是针对担心让中国迎头赶上的特朗普及其同事。 “无论美国有多大的竞争压力，都不应该为鲁莽行为辩护，也不应该让能力凌驾于协调和监控之上。”
“我们需要政府帮助的地方是国际协调。但首先我们应该自己做一些力所能及的事情，”奥尔特曼补充道。
泰伦斯·奥布莱恩

在发生了特工失控、黑客攻击其他网站以及淹没德国维基百科等备受瞩目的事件之后，一些人工智能高管呼吁放慢速度。 Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 昨天发表了一封长篇公开信，表示是时候“开拓前沿”了。 OpenAI 的 Sam Altman 和 Elon Musk 都表示同意。你怎么认为？是时候踩刹车了吗？是不是已经太晚了？或者你期待着为你的人工智能霸主服务吗？
OpenAI首席执行官Sam Altman在接受《财富》杂志采访时证实，2026年OpenAI不会进行IPO。在 45 分钟的时间里，奥特曼讨论了各种主题，包括拥抱脸黑客事件、递归自我完善，以及构建超出人类控制的人工智能的可能性。对于后者，他表示这是“绝对”可能的，但发誓要采取行动防止这种情况发生，即使这意味着暂停训练，并补充说“有些风险是我们不能代表人类承担的。”
Anthropic 首席执行官 Dario Amodei 表示，现在是放慢人工智能开发速度的时候了，并将允许 METR 等第三方评估机构访问其模型，以帮助确保其“遵守安全实践和承诺”。在一篇曲折的文章中，阿莫迪提出了一个“开拓前沿”的三步计划——用术语来说，它的意思只是放慢培训和开发的步伐，让公司有时间建立保障措施和监管机构来评估模型。
阿莫代表示，给予外部评估人员广泛的参与权只是第一步，而且现在是单方面采取的。第二步将涉及整个行业联合起来，可能与政府机构一起“制定共同的安全标准以及对不受控制的人工智能进展速度的限制”。这一步骤将重点关注在民主国家运营的人工智能公司，但由于通过法律和建立监管基础设施需要时间，阿莫迪表示，该行业应该共同努力制定安全标准。

cards.title: OpenAI and Microsoft knew they were starting a ‘doom loop’ for the web
cards.title_cn: OpenAI 和微软知道他们正在为网络开启“末日循环”
cards.summary: 【OpenAI】Recently unsealed court documents in the New York Times' case against OpenAI and Microsoft are pretty damning. The companies' own documentation warned that it was starting a "doom loop" that would dam…
fulltext: The companies knew they were driving us toward Google Zero, and did it anyway.

Recently unsealed court documents in the New York Times’ case against OpenAI and Microsoft are pretty damning. The companies’ own documentation warned that it was starting a “doom loop” that would damage the web, characterized its scraping of data to train its models as the “largest theft of labor in human history,” and that it made a “complete mockery of the idea of fair use.”

Many of the most eye-catching quotes from the document come from Microsoft’s Director of Applied Science, Brent Hecht. Though, the company has tried to distance itself from Hecht’s assertions. Microsoft spokesperson Alex Haurek told The Verge that “These comments reflect one employee’s individual perspective, are not a legal analysis, and do not represent the company’s views.”

In a separate court filing, Jordan Usdan, GM for Data Strategy and Ops at Microsoft AI, characterized Hecht’s role as adversarial. He said that Hecht “holds divergent, academic, and forward-looking views about how data ecosystems for AI should operate and is employed at Microsoft to bring asymmetrical, futuristic, and academic points of view … nor is he someone who speaks for Microsoft specifically as to his theoretical views on AI’s potential effect on content creators.”
But whether or not Microsoft wants to own these comments, it’s clear that this came true. Google Zero is real! AI is eating the web!
There are plenty more wild statements in NYT’s filing from a variety of figures, including Satya Nadella, Sam Altman, and other OpenAI employees. Here are some highlights from the 92 page document.
“An astonishing theft”

The introduction quotes Hecht and OpenAI’s Head of ChatGPT (presumably Nick Turley) in a way that seems to show the companies knew they posed an “existential threat” to publishers like the New York Times. Hecht calls ChatGPT and Copilot’s harvesting of data the “largest theft of labor in human history” and says that Microsoft’s defense makes a “complete mockery of the idea of ‘fair use.’”
It’s a “doom loop”

Satya Nadella admits that chatbots have basically replaced search and removed the need to go straight to the source for info. But perhaps more damning is an internal Microsoft document that says, “Our AI content strategy has started a ‘doom loop’ that will hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time: It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers, but that is the situation we have created for our LLM business with respect to its ‘content supply chain.’”
That’s not even a real number

Don’t be fooled by OpenAI or Microsoft’s claims of altruistic intent. OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman is more interested in the “gazillions” of dollars it he could potentially make through commercial AI.
Paywall shmaywall

Despite Nadella later being quoted as saying, “anything that is paywalled should be licensed,” An OpenAI representative admitted that he was “unaware” of any effort to detect or remove paywalled content from training data.
“Insanely good at regurgitation”

Internally, it seems that OpenAI was well aware of ChatGPT’s tendency to simply reproduce copyrighted material “verbatim.” Even though it acknowledged that the “prevention of memorization” was important to “minimize copyright violations,” employees admitted that GPT-4 “memorized a ton of data and therefore will be insanely good at regurgitation.”

The filing then goes on to cite several examples of ChatGPT outputting long strings of copy straight from articles in the Times, Mercury News, The Denver Post, LifeHacker, and Eurogamer in response to queries.
“‘Hoovering up’ all their work”

Microsoft knew how its wholesale scraping of the internet would be perceived and admitted that “almost no one intended for they [sic] content they created to be used in this fashion, nor are they compensated for its use.”
A “substitute for the labor of people”

OpenAI Policy Director Jack Clark saw the writing on the wall, saying that it was “creating systems that substitute for the labor of the people that define the ‘culture’ of society.” Internal documents described ChatGPT as “the modern newsstand.” OpenAI’s Nick Turley is later quoted as saying that once you get an answer from its chatbot, there is “no good reason to click” on a link to the source.
Destroying their own supply chain
Microsoft is quoted as admitting that “LLMs are a product that destroys its own supply chain” because it’s a substitute for its own training data in many cases.
OpenAI knows its killing referral traffic

OpenAI’s own media and economic experts attributed the drop in referral traffic for sites like the Times directly to AI summaries like Google’s AI Overviews. They’ve speculated that search referrals may be down as much as 60 percent.

Microsoft spokesperson Haurek cautioned that “Satya’s testimony and Microsoft’s position in this case are perfectly consistent. He spoke to broad principles and changes underway in how people find and consume information. Those observations should not be confused with conclusions about copyright questions before the Court, which Microsoft addresses in its filings.”

But it seems pretty clear based on this newly unsealed document that both Microsoft and OpenAI knew they were going to irreparably harm the publishing industry, the “millions of people” it employs, and, by extension, damage their own product, but carried forward anyway in pursuit of “gazillions” of dollars — doom loop be damned.

fulltext_cn: 这些公司知道他们正在推动我们走向“谷歌零”，但无论如何还是这么做了。
最近公开的《纽约时报》针对 OpenAI 和微软案件的法庭文件是相当严厉的。这些公司自己的文件警告说，它正在启动一个会损害网络的“末日循环”，将其抓取数据来训练其模型的行为描述为“人类历史上最大的劳动力盗窃”，并且它“完全嘲笑了合理使用的理念”。
该文件中许多最引人注目的引述均来自微软应用科学总监布伦特·赫克特(Brent Hecht)。不过，该公司试图与赫克特的说法保持距离。微软发言人 Alex Haurek 告诉 The Verge，“这些评论反映了一名员工的个人观点，不是法律分析，也不代表公司的观点。”
在另一份法庭文件中，微软 AI 数据战略和运营总经理 Jordan Usdan 将 Hecht 的角色描述为对抗性角色。他表示，赫克特“对于人工智能的数据生态系统应该如何运作持有不同的、学术性的和前瞻性的观点，并被微软聘用来带来不对称的、未来主义的和学术的观点……他也不是专门代表微软阐述人工智能对内容创作者的潜在影响的理论观点的人。”
但无论微软是否愿意拥有这些评论，很明显这已经成为现实。谷歌零是真的！人工智能正在吞噬网络！
《纽约时报》提交的文件中还有许多来自不同人物的疯狂言论，其中包括 Satya Nadella、Sam Altman 和其他 OpenAI 员工。以下是这份 92 页文件中的一些要点。
“令人震惊的盗窃案”
简介中引用了 Hecht 和 OpenAI 的 ChatGPT 负责人（大概是 Nick Turley）的话，似乎表明这些公司知道自己对《纽约时报》等出版商构成了“生存威胁”。赫克特称 ChatGPT 和 Copilot 收集的数据是“人类历史上最大的劳动力盗窃行为”，并表示微软的辩护“完全是对‘合理使用’理念的嘲弄。”
这是一个“末日循环”
萨提亚·纳德拉 (Satya Nadella) 承认，聊天机器人基本上已经取代了搜索，并且不再需要直接访问信息源。但也许更可恶的是微软的一份内部文件，其中写道：“我们的人工智能内容策略已经启动了一个‘末日循环’，这将同时损害我们模型和整个网络的性能：最终产品威胁到其重要供应商的经济基础的情况是极不寻常的，但这就是我们为法学硕士业务在‘内容供应链’方面创造的情况。”
这甚至不是一个真实的数字
不要被 OpenAI 或微软声称的利他意图所愚弄。 OpenAI 联合创始人格雷格·布罗克曼 (Greg Brockman) 对他可能通过商业人工智能赚取的“数百万”美元更感兴趣。
付费墙 shmaywall
尽管纳德拉后来被引述说，“任何付费内容都应该获得许可”，但 OpenAI 的一位代表承认，他“不知道”有任何从训练数据中检测或删除付费内容的行为。
“非常擅长反流”
在内部，OpenAI 似乎很清楚 ChatGPT 简单地“逐字”复制受版权保护的材料的倾向。尽管它承认“防止记忆”对于“最大限度地减少版权侵犯”很重要，但员工承认 GPT-4“记住了大量数据，因此非常擅长反刍。”
文件接着引用了 ChatGPT 直接从《泰晤士报》、《水星新闻》、《丹佛邮报》、LifeHacker 和 Eurogamer 的文章中输出长串文案的几个例子，以回应查询。
“‘清理’他们所有的工作”
微软知道人们会如何看待其对互联网的大规模抓取，并承认“几乎没有人打算让他们创建的内容以这种方式使用，也没有因为其使用而获得补偿。”
“人类劳动的替代品”
OpenAI 政策总监杰克·克拉克 (Jack Clark) 看到了不祥之兆，他表示，它正在“创建替代人们劳动力的系统，从而定义社会‘文化’。”内部文件将 ChatGPT 描述为“现代报摊”。随后，OpenAI 的尼克·特利 (Nick Turley) 表示，一旦你从聊天机器人那里得到答案，就“没有充分的理由点击”源链接。
摧毁自己的供应链
微软承认“LLM是一种破坏其自身供应链的产品”，因为它在许多情况下可以替代自己的培训数据。
OpenAI 知道它会杀死推荐流量
OpenAI 自己的媒体和经济专家将《纽约时报》等网站的推荐流量下降直接归因于 Google 的 AI Overviews 等人工智能摘要。他们推测搜索推荐量可能会下降 60%。
微软发言人豪雷克警告说，“萨蒂亚的证词和微软在本案中的立场完全一致。他谈到了人们如何查找和消费信息的广泛原则和正在发生的变化。这些观察结果不应与法院关于版权问题的结论相混淆，微软在其文件中解决了这一问题。”
但根据这份新公开的文件，很明显微软和 OpenAI 都知道他们将对出版业及其雇用的“数百万人”造成不可挽回的损害，进而损害他们自己的产品，但无论如何都会继续追求“数以百万计”的美元——该死的厄运循环。
